utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, everybody. Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I'm ready as always, but this time it won't be me who will start. It will be my colleague Meek who will give the introduction to the closing argument, and my colleague Meek will give you the global legal picture of this case. And then I will take it from him and finish the closing argument. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I've thought long and hard about what I can say this morning that might perhaps change your minds or attempt to persuade you in one fashion or another. But first Your Honours I must thank all the people who make this Tribunal possible, those people who are never seen, never seem to have their work satisfactorily recognised, I'd like to thank the translators, the Court reporters, the technical crew, the UN security guards that help us daily, the ushers, the Court staff, and Madam Registrar herself. I would like to take this time to thank Your Honours for your attention and especially for your patience. I trust that the latter will persevere for a little bit longer in this case. Further, Your Honours, I must thank the members of not only my defence team but the members of the Vinko Martinovic Defence team, Mr. Seric, Mr. Par, who have helped me to understand the facts of the war in the former Yugoslavia and the facts of life as it was lived for those unfortunate enough to have lived through such a horrific experience. And I say that in the sense that it is difficult, as Your Honours may well know, if not impossible, to ever have an understanding and a complete grasp of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia and what transpired during that break-up, before that break-up, and after that break-up. First, Your Honours, the accused Mladen Naletilic would incorporate and adopt the legal arguments which have been advanced in the final brief of Vinko Martinovic, which concern international armed conflict, persecution, and superior authority, as the same legal arguments apply to Mr. Naletilic. While there may be some overlapping and duplicity in the arguments advanced, we do incorporate and adopt these by reference. Your Honours, as my learned friend Mr. Scott recently submitted to this Trial Chamber a few days ago, I believe it was the end of last week, this has been a hard-fought trial from both parties, from both sides. From the country from which Mr. Scott and I come, this is only normal in any criminal trial, when the liberty of an accused person is at stake. And in the country from which we grew up practising criminal law, no accused was ever penalised more severely for standing on his presumption of innocence by pleading not guilty, by maintaining that innocence, maintaining his right to silence, and fighting desperately the allegations of the government. It is truly a notion that we, coming from America, are not familiar with, that an accused would be punished more severely for exercising his right to a trial. So, Your Honours, when Mr. Scott states -- or the Prosecutor, excuse me, states in the final brief, under sentencing guidelines for considerations, that Mr. Naletilic did not cooperate with the Prosecutor in any fashion, it must be a foreign argument to him and counter to everything he was brought up with in the criminal procedure of the country from which he comes; namely, Your Honours, it is fundamentally unfair to punish any accused more severely due to the fact that he did not cooperate with the Prosecutor. Why, I ask, would my client cooperate with the Prosecution? Would he cooperate to help the Prosecution deprive him of his liberty? Would he cooperate with the Prosecutor to see that he lives the rest of his natural life in a steel cage? I submit, Your Honours, that it is completely natural and normal for any innocent person to fight for his or her liberty. That liberty is the most precious of commodities and in this specific case, unfortunately, it is a fight for the very life of my client. Mr. Naletilic unfortunately does not have very good health, as the record can attest, and nearly any term of incarceration for him, should he be convicted, will be nothing less than a life sentence. Briefly, Your Honour, on the subject of my client's health, the Prosecution states in their final brief that according to the Simic sentencing judgement, which just was rendered a few weeks ago, the ill health of the accused is not a mitigating factor. However, Your Honours, you should not be fooled by this half truth, as later in the same judgement, the Trial Chamber stated clearly that ill health is a special circumstance in sentencing considerations and may be taken into account. Regarding sentencing, while I'm on this subject briefly, it is submitted, Your Honours, that there must be some equality and some proportionality in sentencing in this Tribunal. The record is clear, Your Honours may take judicial notice that General Radoslav Krstic, the commander of the drina corps, who was found guilty of genocide in the Srebrenica massacres of up to 8.000 young Muslim men in a one-week period in 1995, was sentenced to approximately 43 years. While in this case, Your Honours, the Prosecution asks you that if convicted, Mr. Naletilic be sentenced to 35 years. Mr. Naletilic was not charged in this case with even one murder, let alone genocide, of which General Krstic was convicted. A Chinese proverb says that if vengeance, if it is vengeance you're seeking, dig two graves instead of one. It appears to me, Your Honour and it appears to the Defence of Mr. Naletilic that in fact the Prosecution in this case is seeking vengeance. And it is submitted, Your Honours, that if Mr. Naletilic is found guilty, which we believe is not proper under the evidence and the law, that this sentence requested by the Prosecution is completely outside the bounds of any reason or logic. Your Honours, another example of the Prosecution misstating the evidence and shaving the truth or the law can be seen in the Prosecution final brief, page 12 to 13, when it is stated that Prosecution Witness R, the French journalist, as you will recall, had found it difficult to move around Mostar. And that due to that difficulty, Mr. Naletilic gave him a paper which allowed the witness to move freely around the Croat part of Mostar. In fact, Your Honours, if you will look at the transcript closely, if you will look at the evidence of Witness R closely, you will see that Mr. Naletilic never -- never -- gave witness Witness R any paper. He merely gave Witness R a name. Upon giving him that name, Witness R was able to gain a laissez-faire pass, and he gained that pass from an individual from Mostar, an individual who was in a high military position with the HVO in Mostar by the name of Zlatan Jelic. Mr. President, I would ask kindly to go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must at this time ask you that if there was anything that I personally did or that this Defence team of Mr. Naletilic did during the course of this trial which might have offended you in any manner, in any manner whatsoever, please accept my apologies, the apologies from the Defence team, and please, Your Honours, I beseech you, do not -- do not hold this against Mr. Naletilic. Your Honours, it is truly a pleasure and it is my honour to represent Mr. Naletilic. In my opinion, it is the highest calling of a lawyer to represent a citizen accused of a crime. There is nothing higher in the practice of law than standing between the citizen accused of a crime and the might of the government, in this case the Prosecution. It is not often -- no, it is very rare indeed that any lawyer has the opportunity to represent a citizen accused in a war crimes trial, and as I have stated, it is always a honour to represent any person accused by the government. In this case, Your Honours, the Prosecutor for all practical purposes, and by analogy, stands in the same shoes as the government. The Prosecution in this Tribunal, not unlike the government Prosecutors around the globe, has tremendous power and a seemingly endless supply of logistical help. The Prosecution has a vast and huge means at her disposal to accomplish the ends she desires. Behind the scenes of this courtroom, Your Honours, there is an army of support staff for the Prosecution. There are investigators, interpreters, translators, experts, analysts, and a budget to back them up. Unfortunately, Your Honours, what you see here -- what you see here, is what you get from the Defence. We do have one investigator, part time, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we do not have the resources at our hands that the Prosecution has. However, and thankfully, the concept of equality of arms is sacred in this Tribunal. Equally, sacred is the concept and the theory of presumption of innocence and burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. While the accused before this Tribunal do not have to, nor are they obligated, to prove their innocence, from the perspective of an American lawyer, I must confess that it sometimes seems that this is not the case. For example, when one looks at the language of the Statute of the International Tribunal, adopted 25 May, 1993, as amended 13 May, 1998, it states, "Having been established by the Security Council, acting under chapter 7 of the charter of the United Nations, the International Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991." From the mere reading of that language, it appears that those citizens who find themselves as accused before this Tribunal have already been prejudged. Why does the language state, "Persons responsible for serious crimes or serious violations?" Why doesn't the Statute refer to those persons alleged to be responsible? Further, Your Honours, Article 1 goes on to state, "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations." Again, Your Honours, the language itself seems to presuppose a pre-judgment of those accused coming before this Tribunal. There are other examples to be found in the wording of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but the point is simply that this Tribunal has been viewed by some legal scholars, and observers, as being political in nature and not a serious legal body. Some, in fact, might state that this Tribunal is nothing more than an attempt to relieve and alleviate the collective guilt of the United States, Europe, Great Britain and the western world for not stopping the blood shed, violence, and tragedy in the former Yugoslavia at a time when it was in the power of the west to do so. As such, it is submitted that this Tribunal is often viewed as a political institution with the Prosecution arm that has unfettered power and where the institution itself is permeated with a "we must convict" attitude. Your Honours, one such commentator, Robert M. Hayden, professor of anthropology and law, University of Pittsburg, and director at the centre for Russian and east European studies in an article published in the Cleveland state law review which was entitled, "Biased justice, human rightsism and the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia" observed that the ICTY delivers a justice that is biased with prosecutorial decisions based on national characteristics of the accused, rather than on the available evidence indicating exactly what he has done." Certainly, it is submitted that it can be argued that Mr. Naletilic would not be in this Tribunal at this moment for the last two years or more, had not the Republic of Croatia and/or those in power that deemed it expedient to serve him up to the OTP in order to save other much-higher political, civic, or military figures. When Mr. Hayden commentates or opines that in fact there is an attitude in this Tribunal, in this institution, that we must convict, I must point out one example. This example is the Kupreskic case. I implore the Trial Chamber to look closely at the Kupreskic appeals case, which I believe supports this notion. In that case, the Appeals Chamber had the wisdom and courage, the independence and judicial integrity to correct an obviously skewed judgement, a judgement that was rendered in a Trial Chamber. There, Your Honours, three of the convicted accused were released on appeal, after the Appeals Chamber found that no reasonable finder of fact could conclude guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on the evidence presented. Further, Your Honours, in that case, the Trial Chamber had found guilt on a charge never alleged in the indictment, no notice had ever been given to the accused that he would be tried for such a charge. However, Your Honours, in the end, justice was served in that instance. Likewise, the international community was served, and I submit, Your Honours, that the memory of the victims was also served. The memory of the victims of the tragedies in the former Yugoslavia were served for a very simple reason: Innocent men were not wrongfully convicted in that case. We submit, Your Honours, that it takes an independent, conscientious judicial panel to make such a decision in the face of what we have all heard to be the cries of the international community for justice. Justice at what price, Your Honours? Mr. Hayden goes on to opine that, "Judicial decisions by the ICTY render it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for an accused to obtain a fair trial while the Tribunal has also shown a lack of interest in the investigation of potential prosecutorial misconduct." Additionally, it is questioned in that article just why the Tribunal actions that so clearly violate fundamental fairness towards the defendants are not the subject of much concern by those who profess to support human rights. The author of that article, Mr. Hayden goes on to state that, "The politicisation of the ICTY's Prosecutor's office is especially troubling, in light of the extraordinary deference that the judges of the Tribunal afford the Prosecutor." Your Honours, when one considers the basic goals of a War Crimes Tribunal, the question may easily be asked: How many people would really afford the presumption of innocence to leaders such as Hermann Goering or Slobodan Milosevic? How many would, Your Honours? Why give such criminals a forum in the first place? Why spend money and time to hear their stories? Thus, Your Honours, it may be said that if any trial is worth conducting, then it is worth conducting fairly and courts that apply the above principle rigorously become stronger, not weaker. In the same vein, it is understandable that courts must display, by example, that they are governed by law rather than by passions or politics of any particular case. Justice Robert Jackson of the United States Supreme Court, one of the architects of the Nuremberg Tribunal, in a speech he gave in April of 1945, concerning the greatly debated problem of what to do with the Nazi leaders when and if they were captured, said that a political and military decision could be taken to simply execute them, based on a number of political, practical and policy considerations. However, Justice Jackson then discussed the alternative option, to wit Justice Jackson said: "If good faith trials are sought, that is another matter. All experience teaches that there are certain things you cannot do under the guise of judicial trial. Courts try cases but cases also try courts. You must put no man on trial before anything that is called a court under the forms of judicial proceedings if you are not willing to see him freed if not proven guilty." This was taken from the book called, "The Anatomy of the Nuremberg Trials," published in 1992 by Alfred Knopf in New York. What Justice Jackson was merely observing was that any body that -- denoted a court of law should not be used to rubber stamp convictions and sentences. That could be accomplished through political channels, we all know that. A court of law, properly defined, must be ready for a judicial trial based on the presumption of innocence and always open-minded to the possibility of acquittal, for it must be remembered that not every alleged war criminal, merely because he or she is indicted, is guilty as charged. Your Honours, I believe that history will judge this Tribunal by the way this Tribunal judges the accused who are tried before it. It will, Your Honours, in the end, be judged by the fairness in which it dispenses justice and the process it affords the accused before, after, and especially during the proceedings. I must confess, Your Honours, that this last 14 months has been difficult for me, coming from a country with a strong, albeit short, history of judicial watch-dogging. This judicial watch-dogging operates to ensure that the person accused by the government is accorded the process due him before, until, and unless he is found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. There are basic, fundamental, civilised human rights that he or she will receive a fair trial, the right to confront his or her accusers, the right to know specifically the nature and extent of the charges against him, and the right to not be convicted on any evidence which does not rise to the level of beyond a reasonable doubt. This has been difficult for me from the perspective of having to sit by and watch as incredible, horrible hearsay evidence is admitted against my client in both live testimony and in the form of documentary evidence. Documents which are admitted with no real meaningful foundation, no authenticity, no chain of custody, and no reliability -- at least coming from the standpoint the safeguards under which I practise criminal law in the United States, and the safeguards built into most common law criminal jurisprudence. Your Honours, I understand that this type of tenuous evidence is admissible under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Practice and Procedure, in this Tribunal, and I understand further, Your Honours, that even when documents such as this are admitted, it does not automatically follow that the Trial Chamber must give them any weight or will give them any weight. However, it's still to me seems fundamentally unfair when viewed in the scope of a criminal proceeding where a person's liberty is at stake. For liberty, Your Honours, is like the air we breathe; we take it for granted until we don't have it any longer or we begin to lose it. Were this a case where the ultimate judgement is only for monetary remuneration, for a personal injury or contractual damages, for instance, then perhaps one could say it was more fundamentally fair given what was at stake. However, it seems only just and fair to demand more credible evidence than that routinely submitted by the Prosecution and accepted into evidence by the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal. A glowing example of this can be seen from the final argument of my learned colleague, Mr. Scott, yesterday. My learned friend stated that he would recall in substantial measure, six important Prosecution witnesses to give the Chamber an overall feel of the case. While waiting with bated breath for the recounting of these six important witnesses, it turned out that they consisted of only two witnesses who one could actually say were fact witnesses. Those two witnesses were Witness O and the mufti. Three others were by and large witnesses who gathered their information from other sources, LL was a Spanish officer, Van der Grinten a Dutch officer with the ECMM, and Sir Martin Garrod a British officer. These military witnesses came before this Tribunal and testified about events they never personally observed. Their testimony was largely based on reports they drafted from reports they received from the field. These field reports in turn were based on informants unknown to the accused, unknown to the accused's attorneys, and most likely unknown to the witnesses themselves. Most of the reports they testified about and testified from were classified C-2. Your Honours will recall that C-2 was the lowest class of reliability when it came to reporting, and this was according to Witness JJ, a military intelligence officer from Spain, or in layman's terms a spy. That's what he was. The testimony pointed out by my learned friend, Mr. Scott, that was based on these three witnesses' own personal experience and observation can be boiled down to dinner conversation or cocktail talk. This is especially true, Your Honours, of Witness LL, whose testimony was nothing more than mere speculation after a brief meeting with Mr. Naletilic and Prosecution Exhibit 325, a document which in the body of the same states that it was derived, "According to intelligence received." We must ask, Your Honours, from where, when, and from whom was this information received? Van der Grinten's testimony, likewise, was based in part -- and part what the Prosecutor wants Your Honours to believe was based on P484, a meeting with a Mr. Puljic. If Your Honours will at Exhibit P484 with any kind of scrutiny, you will see that Mr. Puljic had stated -- or excuse me, that Mr. Van der Grinten had stated that Mr. Puljic, "Seemed to be more friendly than his HVO colleagues," and apparently Van der Grinten and those working under him stated, "We think he has told us the truth." I wonder, Your Honours, what "We think he has told us the truth" means. Does that mean that he could have told the truth? Does that mean that he maybe told the truth? Does that mean he might have told the truth? It certainly, Your Honours, doesn't mean that he told the truth beyond a reasonable doubt, and yet we are daily and have weekly listened to testimony such as this brought into this Trial Chamber in order to convict Mr. Naletilic. Sir Martin Garrod's testimony, which the Prosecutor eliminates is derived from a lunch he claims to have shared with Mr. Naletilic at the home of Witness NH, a defence Witness. If you will recall, Your Honours, Witness NH testified that while Garrod and Naletilic had lunch at his home, they had never lunched together at his home. Further, Your Honours, NH shared with the Trial Chamber his observation that Mr. -- Sir Martin Garrod, who NH saw frequently, liked "to have a glass too many and that it was very nice to talk to him." The mufti on the other hand, while not prone to excessive drinking of alcohol, can certainly not be said to be unbiased in any fashion. And if the Chamber remembers, the mufti could not even speak the truth about the Islamic flag shown in a video of a celebration of the 44 Muslim mountain Brigade of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - one of the most fundamental Islamic military organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. To put it very nicely and civilly, even Judge Clark was disappointed with his reply concerning the Islamic flag. What else -- what else, it must be asked, did the mufti distort or fabricate in his testimony? On the other hand, Your Honours, Witness O was only one of two Prosecution witnesses who could even place Mladen Naletilic with Mate Boban. Yet the Prosecution still maintains that they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were close associates and that Mr. Naletilic carried out Mate Boban's orders. The only other witness to place Mate Boban with Mr. Naletilic won't even be mentioned in this argument, as her testimony was completely unbelievable and was further refuted by Witness NC, who was at the Easter party at the Ero hotel in Mostar in 1993. Finally, Your Honours, the sixth important witness my learned friend spoke about was none other than President Franjo Tudjman. This witness has come from the grave to apparently give evidence before this lofty Tribunal. I ask Your Honours, how can it be deemed equitable, how can it be deemed to be just, how can it be deemed to be fair for the accused to defend himself against such blatant hearsay, which is unchallengeable and is without any means to confront the witness? Yet the Prosecution in this case relies most heavily on these purported presidential transcripts to prove the existence of an international armed conflict beyond a reasonable doubt. At this point, Your Honours, I must address briefly the truly important witnesses for the Prosecution in this case. Those important witnesses, Your Honour, are the two thiefing, murdering, lying Germans, Falk Simang and Ralf Mrachacz. One needs only to look at the foot notes of the Prosecution's final brief to see that they are relying heavily, heavily on the testimony of Falk Simang and to some minor, lesser degree, Ralf Mrachacz. It must be remembered, Your Honours, that the testimony even from Mrachacz was that it was Mladen Naletilic who was instrumental in the turning in of this murderer to the German authorities when he finally learned of what Mrachacz had done, and he only learned it later, much later. In the closing argument yesterday, my learned friend implored Your Honours of the accused, "Don't let them have victory, don't let them have their victory." My learned friend thereafter asked you to convict on all charges but whatever you do, Your Honours, "Don't let them have their victory." I simply ask Your Honours, what is dishonourable about this Trial Chamber or any legitimate court of law, for that matter, entering a judgement of not guilty if, upon due consideration of the facts and the law, the Prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt? What, pray tell, is improper about that? A reasonable doubt is a real doubt, based upon reasonable -- based upon reason and common sense after careful and impartial consideration of all the evidence in the case. This should not, nor can it be based on sympathy, pity or compassion, as my learned friend seemed to be asking of Your Honours at the close of his argument yesterday. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt is proof of such a convincing character that you would be willing to rely and act upon it without hesitation in the most important of your affairs. We all make decisions in our life every day, all the time. We buy homes, we buy cars, we make employment decisions. But would we hesitate if Falk Simang or Ralf Mrachacz tried to sell us an used car for a life insurance policy, for example? Would we hesitate? The issue, the final issue, is in fact exactly that: Would you hesitate? If the testimony that you heard creates any hesitation in believing, then there is a reasonable doubt, I submit. I would like to quote from a losing argument made by an American lawyer by the name of Edward Bennett Williams in a trial, particularly this closing argument made by Edward Bennett Williams concerns these two star witnesses of the Prosecution. Mr. Williams said: "I just want to say two last things. You know, I think in life you can bargain for and buy almost anything. You can bargain for and buy mansions and villas and priceless works of art. You can bargain for and buy fine jewellery and all the creature comforts that you can conjure up in your mind, but thank God there are some things you can't buy and you can't bargain for. You can't buy or bargain for wisdom. You can't buy or bargain for justice, because if you do, what you get is injustice. You can't buy or bargain for love, because if you do, it isn't love that you get. And you can't buy or bargain for truth, because it isn't truth that you get. It's testimony with a cloud of suspicion hanging over it. You can buy and you can bargain for testimony," and that is what the government did in this case, that is why their case is in the state it is at the present time. This case is entitled United States versus a defendant; this case is entitled the Prosecution versus Mr. Naletilic. But I want to tell you something: The United States will win this case. The United States will win this case. I saw one day on the walls of a courthouse in the oldest courthouse in England, the words, "In this hallowed place of justice, the Crown never loses because when liberty of an English man is preserved against false witnesses, the Crown wins." After travelling for over 22 years across America in courthouses all over that country, and now for over a year in this Tribunal in The Hague, I can tell you, Your Honours, that the Prosecution never loses, because when the liberty and reputation of a citizen accused is preserved against false testimony, giving of false testimony, the Prosecution wins. Justice wins the day against the false testimony. My father, Your Honours, was a lawyer, was a district court judge for 16 years. His father, my grandfather, was a lawyer. My father's brother was a lawyer. My father's sister was a lawyer. And my father taught me this when I was but a child. He explained to me, "Chris, it's easy to be a Prosecutor. The Prosecutor never loses." I said, "Dad, what do you mean?" He said, "The Prosecutor never loses. If he tries a case -- if he tries a case, and he gets a conviction, then he has won. If he tries a case and the judgement comes back not guilty, then justice has been served and he also wins." Having been both a Prosecutor and a criminal defence lawyer, Your Honours, I submit that being a Prosecutor is simply a much easier task than that which we have before us. Your Honours, the Defence would implore the Trial Chamber to disregard and give no weight to such tenuous, hearsay evidence in the name of international justice and in the memory of the victims of the horrible wars in the former Yugoslavia, as it would be a disservice for any person to be convicted of such war crimes on evidence which is not credible and which does not rise to the level of beyond a reasonable doubt in the names of the victims and in the name of the international community. In fact, Your Honours, the Defence submits most respectfully that in the very name of the victims and the international community, this Trial Chamber must afford these accused a fair trial in all respects. Indeed, the victims and the international community demand no less. Please consider, Your Honours, while you're deliberating the fate of my client, Mr. Naletilic, how you would feel, how you personally would feel, if you were the accused, or you had a loved one or a close friend or family member who was an accused. Ask yourself, "How would I like it if I stood accused and the Prosecution was bringing in hearsay evidence, evidence based on rumour, innuendo, gossip, documents which we don't know where -- which you don't know where they came from, documents that have no authenticity. Please put yourself in the shoes of Mr. Naletilic when you're deliberating his fate. Where is Mr. Meek going with this, you might ask. Simply, Your Honour, that probably -- no, most likely, the most important phase of this trial is about to begin, the phase where Your Honours begin your deliberations on the facts, apply them to the law, and while not -- I say not paying lip service to the accused's fundamental right to the presumption of innocence, also and always bearing in mind that the accused has nothing to prove, has a right to silence, making the Prosecutor live up to their burden of proof, their duty to prove each element of each crime beyond a reasonable doubt. If you can do this based on credible evidence, not evidence which is based on what the witnesses heard or knew because everybody knew, based on documents which contain multiple hearsay, rumour, speculation, and innuendo, in this case these documents are largely coming from AID, and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the victims who want someone, anyone, to pay the price for their suffering. If you can do this, Your Honours, then we submit that at the end of the day you will conclude, with clear consciences, that the Prosecution has failed in its burden of proof, that there is a reasonable doubt as to the accused's guilt, and therefore you will render a verdict of not guilty of the charges leveled against Mr. Naletilic. Your Honours, the burden of -- and quantum of proof in a criminal case, and at this Tribunal, is on the Prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, upon consideration of all the facts, evidence and circumstances of the case, that the accused is guilty of the crimes charged. Since the accused in a criminal case, and in this case, is presumed to be innocent until the contrary is proved, this requires the Prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt every fact necessary to establish the crimes were committed and that the accused committed them. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt, Your Honours, excludes every reasonable hypothesis except guilt of the accused. The burden to prove each and every material element of a crime never shifts from the Prosecution to the accused. It is a fundamental, basic tenet in criminal law that the Prosecution must prove the case set forth in the indictment in all material parts beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the finders of fact in their analysis of the evidence, viewed in the light most favourable to the accused, must find, in order to convict, that all elements of each crime charged has been established by such a degree of proof. The rationale behind this rule is obvious, and this is a requirement, and it is very important requirement to reduce the risk that an innocent person will be convicted. And it must be and has been incorporated into the concept of fundamental fairness, fair trial, and equality of arms. As has been stated, it is better to acquit nine guilty men than to convict one innocent man. For this reason, Your Honours, the Defence implores you to put the Prosecution on strict proof of each and every element of the various crimes charged before you convict. When the dust settles, Your Honour, and at the end of the day, after you have carefully evaluated all the evidence, both the testimony adduced in this courtroom and the documents admitted, I ask you to return a judgement that will be consistent with my client and international justice winning against false witnesses, and that would be a judgement of not guilty. Your Honours, I must ask, and I would ask you to also ask this question: If Mr. Naletilic was - as the Prosecutor alleges, and has desperately tried to prove - a military or civic, civilian superior, and a high-ranking HVO member, why was he never at any meeting of high-ranking officials of the HVO or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Why, for example, was Mr. Naletilic, who it is claimed was a superior to Mr. Martinovic, not sent a copy of Prosecutor Exhibit 562.2? If you look at that Prosecution document, Your Honours, and if you look at a multitude of other Prosecution documents that are similar to Exhibit 562.2, and 562.2, in fact, was a report concerning Mr. Martinovic and alleged wrong-doings, this report was sent, was sent, Your Honours, to Mr. Jelic, and the Defence submits for a good reason this report was sent to Mr. Jelic. Your Honours, this report and the numerous other documents entered into evidence by the Prosecution and accepted by this Trial Chamber were sent to Mr. Martinovic's real commander, his real superior, and it was not Mr. Naletilic. Your Honours, this is but one example of documents speaking about purported bad deeds of Mr. Martinovic, but these documents were never sent to Mr. Naletilic, his alleged superior. We submit, Your Honours, that it is illogical, ill conceived, and bordering on absurdity for Mr. Naletilic to have been the commander or superior officer of Mr. Martinovic and never receiving reports of alleged crimes or bad acts that Mr. Martinovic was involved in in the city of Mostar. In closing, I would ask the Trial Chamber to look at another factor. If Mladen Naletilic is who they say he is, who the Prosecution says he is, why is he not charged with war crimes in the conflict with the Serbs in 1992 when he really did command the Convicts Battalion? There were certainly no Serbs living in Mostar at the end of 1993. If he is who they say he is, why do we not find him at meetings with high-ranking HVO and high-ranking HZ HB officials? If he is who they say he is, why do we not find him in any meetings with Franjo Tudjman? The Prosecution witness who came back from the grave to testify against Mr. Naletilic. If he is who they say he is, why do we not have documents from Mate Boban to Mr. Naletilic? If he is who they say he is, why was he not even a member of the political party, the HDZ? If he is who they say he is, why do we not have any documents admitted into this Trial Chamber from Tudjman to him? If he is who they say he is, why are there so many documents signed by Ivan Andabak, not signed by Ivan Andabak "for" Mladen Naletilic but just signed Ivan Andabak? Why, Your Honour, has there been no evidence, absolutely no evidence, brought into this Chamber that Mr. Naletilic allowed or authorised Ivan Andabak, the commander of the Convicts Battalion in 1993, to sign his name? We submit, Your Honours, it's because Mr. Naletilic never gave such authorisation, never had the authority to give such authorisation, never had any knowledge that Mr. Andabak was signing documents which still had stamped or typed on them, "Mladen Naletilic, commander of the Convicts Battalion." Those documents, we submit, arose from 1992 in the conflict with the Serbs. If, Your Honours, Mr. Naletilic is who the Prosecution says he is, why are there so many orders and reports coming to Ivan Andabak as commander of the Convicts Battalion? The evidence has been clear, Your Honours, that after Mr. Naletilic retired due to his ill health in the fall of 1992, that many people still referred to him as "General" or "commander." So what? My father was a district court judge. Many of his friends were district court judges who had retired. And we all referred to them as "judge" even after they had retired. I have friends in America who are retired senators and I still call them "senator" when I meet them. What evidence is it that somebody would call Mr. Naletilic or refer to Mr. Naletilic as "general" after he had retired? We submit there is no relevance to that and no nexus to any of the connected charges that the Prosecution wants you to believe. I submit, Your Honours, that ten years from now, if I run into one of you in some airport or on the street, I'm going to say, "Judge. How are you, Judge?" Whether you're still a Judge, whether you've been a Judge, whether you're retired. When I do that, Your Honour, it doesn't mean that you're still a Judge. We all know that. Your Honour, the facts and evidence are simply just not present for a foundation of a guilty verdict. While the Prosecution has tried and attempted to lay on Mr. Naletilic's doorstep the ethnic cleansing which occurred in Herzegovina in 1993, it is respectfully submitted, Your Honours, that that dog just won't hunt. It did not happen. The Defence respectfully requests that Your Honours enter the only proper legal judgement based on the laws and the facts, and that is not guilty. Your Honours, it is truly my pleasure to have been part of this Tribunal. And it is truly a pleasure to have represented Mr. Naletilic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we will make a break here, and we will resume the closing arguments after the break. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall start with my part of the closing argument, following up on the words of my learned friend, Mr. Meek. May it please the Court, for the last time in this trial I shall address you as the international criminal Tribunal. It is my honour for the last time before you to say and summarise Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. everything that has been happening in this courtroom over the period of the last 14 months. After the 14 months of the procedure, counting also the time of last year when depositions were taken, at the end of this long, demanding, strenuous, and stressful trial, the Defence is now aware of many things and has concluded many things. First and foremost, we are now aware -- and I should immediately start talking about my client rather than wait, as Mr. President has always said that my most interesting arguments came towards the end, I'm going to change that. I have changed a lot of things over the night from yesterday to today. I'm not going to repeat anything that we have written in the closing brief. And after what we heard yesterday, I'm just going to say something about the exhibits that the OTP referred to yesterday. The Defence, as I've already said, has become aware of many things. First and foremost, that the name of my client, Mladen Naletilic, has been abused, that in this courtroom, various circumstances were based on everything, and the only thing that they were not based on is his criminal responsibility. His place has never been in this courtroom. This is the light at the end of the tunnel that I saw yesterday. I am sorry that the -- we did not have more time, because there is so much more we could have done, so many more witnesses we could have called if we only had the time. Why? Because for the first time in the history of this world, the world justice is being done. We believe that we will be able to change the mind set that prevails in this building. Why? Because of justice. And now we come to the thing that I will mostly address, the thing that we have become aware of, at the end of this trial, at the moment when I am in the position to summarise the whole procedure. And whatever we said during the trial, whatever we said in -- about the acquittal, whatever has been said, I'm not going to repeat. I'm just going to say that the Defence is aware of the counts in the indictment, the indictment is a result of the unilateral approach of the OTP to the events which took place during 1993. To be more precise, between April 1993 and February, 1994. My colleague, Meek, has been the person who has inspired me throughout this trial, because every day when we left this courtroom, we started debating, and I started worrying, and every time I would say, "Is this really possible? What are we to expect, if such a highly educated colleague from a developed country does not understand things that are absolutely notorious and well-known to us, the things that we have lived with all our lives and for which we never expected we would have to discuss them in this courtroom?" Obviously, my colleague, Meek, very soon started understanding things from the more general to the more specific. Why was I worried? Because my colleague, Meek, was not the only foreigner in this courtroom, and I realised that it was taking him a long time to understand things. How long would it have taken me if I was a Prosecutor or a Judge in a case dealing with events that would have taken place a long way from here? How long would it have taken me to understand? Why am I concerned with that? I'm concerned because I have come to realise the way the OTP works. The OTP, according to the Statute of this Tribunal, has to be objective. It cannot and it shouldn't present only the things in its favour, only the things which seem to be true to them. However, this is exactly what they did. We are aware, and we have the proof of that, that the indictment was raised in 1998, and the OTP either created a picture or was given that picture, and then in that picture, they started looking for proof in order to be able to prove that the picture is true to the fact. That was my first reason to be astonished, maybe because I come from the Roman law. Although there shouldn't be any difference between the Anglo-Saxon and the Roman law because both seek for the truth. This Tribunal does not linger in the air beyond the -- beyond time and space. It is here, on this earth. We only have a certain procedure that has relied more on the Anglo-Saxon law than on the Roman law, but this Tribunal, which seeks for international justice, it has to respect all the legal norms that have existed from the time of the ancient Rome to the present day, and the legal principles from that time to today are always the same. We need to find the truth, and then base our judgement on the truth, whatever the truth may be. The OTP in developing the picture of the truth, of their truth, even files the indictment and then the race for evidence starts. How is one to prove that indictment? Well, if they are short on evidence, then problems start, and then the Prosecutor's Office, with the power unheard of in the history of legal civilisation, which acts independently and is free of any control mechanism which exists in any domicile law in any country in the world, the so-called control of the indictment or a higher instance which will control the work of a lower instance. And then if that is so, this is how things go. These uncooperative, these don't know this. And I find myself in difficulties because of... Now, listen, we have realised that basically everybody cooperates with the OTP in so far as that is concerned because the OTP has the access wherever it pleases to gain such an access. In 14 months, together with my two colleagues, sitting here and investing a superhuman effort, I had absolutely no time to sit in the archives at the same time, be it in Zagreb and even less so in Sarajevo, even less so in the President's office, even less so in Madrid where SpaBat documents are, or ECMM. I even don't have -- cannot afford it. I do not have an investigator to do it, nor have I been approved one at the time when the proceedings started. And moreover, Your Honours, I cannot get to the President's office. The BH Army, I received a letter, which I have submitted to you, and in which the Minister of Defence tells me that his deputy will not allow him to authorise me to get into the BH Army's archive. Moreover, we also received a letter from that man, the same man from the Bosniak part in the Ministry of Defence, in the federation, I'm talking about the ministry in the federation, the entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the entity of the Croats and Muslims, if the minister is a Croat, then his deputy must be a Bosniak or vice versa and another letter which I have also submitted to you said that they had consulted the OTP, and the OTP said, "Well, no, you can't really do things this way." I mean, for me to be allowed the access to this, that I have to seek such an access through the Tribunal, and at the same time, the gentleman from the Prosecution get in where they please and how they please and when they please. As for -- as regards the army archives, I -- they procrastinated by resorting to a political game. The HVO archive, again, I couldn't get there because I couldn't be in two places at one and the same time. And after all, nobody knows what the size of this archive is, how many documents there are and what kind of documents are. But the OTP knows it all, and now what? Imagine that you are on the stage and somebody releases fog, and then from this fog emerges somebody that we are supposed to see. It's usually on the stage. A kind of a show. And then through this fog we see something emerging. And that is what the Prosecutor does; they release fog. And now we are left to wonder what is it that they offer us in this fog? Yesterday, the closing arguments were heard happened after 14 months, and after daily questions of -- asked by myself and my colleagues, is this it? Is this all? I kept saying, "Well, this must be it. Because there can be nothing else because it does not exist because it's simply not -- because one cannot simply fabricate something that is not, that does not exist, one cannot invent a document even though I'll come to documents later, but one cannot just invent a document to show that Mr. Naletilic is a general. Why cannot it be invented? Because we have established once and for all in these proceedings that every rank, and because their ranks go began to be conferred in the HVO in 1994 and every such rank had to be announced publicly. Otherwise, it was invalid. So if a commander is being conferred upon a rank, it must be carried by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Official Gazette, which publishes every law and every decree. Well, if it existed, do you think that the OTP wouldn't be waving with it? They like to wave in the air with all sorts of documents and papers. But they didn't because it doesn't exist because it never existed. Do you really think that they would have failed to show any order to prove that had my client bean the commander of the Convicts Battalion, and let us at least -- let them at least tell us that there are documents about his appointment to a particular post but they have not come up with this. So how and why? And of course when it doesn't exist, you can say freely, "Well, he was that." And is it really up to the Defence to produce evidence about the HVO structure, about the structure of the police? Why didn't the OTP do that and say, "Look, this is -- this is the structure of the HVO. This is the chain of -- the command, let's call it the chain of command and that's where Mr. Naletilic is it in this." But they didn't do it because they are quite happy with this situation and that's what the Prosecution always does when they release fog, because they think they can make a quick buck from that. They think that by showing us stories and documents or ignoring, disregarding, some very important facts, they will produce some effect, even an albeit a small one but it's somewhere there. And if it's there then perhaps it could be here. And just don't let him, please, get off. Sentence him -- and perhaps it doesn't matter if it's a year or what, it doesn't matter but just condemn him to something because you can't think -- I can't lose -- I can't possibly lose, what would it be after 14 months, after all these vast amounts of money spent, the money of the international community, and I'm also a member of it and all of us here, after all of this money that was spent, after all these little things, what is it that has been proven? What was this argument that was used and proffered to the world, Tribunal? None, no argument, not a real tangible proof, not a single factual proof. And if that is so, then let's put politics on trial and let's get into political stories. And there is again not a single shred of evidence for that, and I do not know whether the OTP is indeed asking this Court to try politics, to try political attitude, political views, can't be, then let's talk about history and the OTP, is that what the OTP is asking you, to try history, believing that your judgement will change a historical fact or the course of history? Your Honours, you will not be trying history, and even if you did that, history cannot be changed -- judgements do not change history. Historians, historiographers do that, not courts, not judgements, and why is it -- is it the -- so much, why did we waste so much time to discuss here some things which are common knowledge? Such as, for instance, that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a thing non-extant. Remember how much time we wasted on this, and yet it suffices to open the Dayton Accords and read it. And then it becomes absolutely clear that it does not exist, and then it is absolutely clear that the Prosecutor cannot write that the source of a document is the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he does it nevertheless, and does it persistently. Why? Because he's concealing the true source and doesn't know what to name it, and that is the AID. But placing trust in your fairness, in your love for truth, it will be fair for all the documents which are sourced to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to be even read, to refuse to read them, because the OTP couldn't give you the source because it doesn't have it. How much time did we waste, Your Honours, to show not Bosnia as many notably the OTP which uses this word, because Bosnia doesn't exist. It has never existed as Bosnia. It is a state which was recognised for the first time in its history, which emerged for the first time, recognised, with its external borders, external borders, not its internal political order, in 1992. And the moment when it was recognised with these external borders, it disintegrated inside that very same moment. We shall come to that later but in my closing argument, without spending too much time on it, because I know that you will read it all, I know that you will analyse it all, and in this closing argument, I do not wish to tax your patience by repeating facts and especially not by reading documents to you because I have other things to do and other arguments to proffer, except to read some very questionable documents. And let me conclude this subject. When this state disintegrated, it has never come together to this day, never. And that is common knowledge. It is a well-known fact. Everybody knows it. Everybody except the OTP. Why they refuse to accept this fact, I've understood very well, because it is the alliance and we shall speak about this further, how did it come about and why the OTP is doing this. Yesterday, in its closing argument, the OTP says the Bosnian president, until the very last moment, until the very last second, there is not even the minutest hope that they might become objective, because the Bosnian president doesn't exist, Alija Izetbegovic was not one, nor was there such a thing as the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I hope that we've established even this widely known fact. There is an institution which is called the President of the Presidency, and this is rotating post, that is -- and I will ask the interpreters to help me. It was the chairman of the Presidency, and that was a rotating post. And he was the first amongst the equals, the primus inter pares when discharging that office. And there is no doubt that he has not been discharging lawfully since 1992 when, during his second consecutive term of office, under the then constitution and set of rules, he had to leave that post and didn't, but we'll come back to that later. I hope there will be time for it, but these are just a few sketchy details. What has been bothering me all this time, all my discussion was Mr. Meek, all that I had gone through perhaps we've really been wasting time going about, talking about these notorious historical facts. And I've been asking Mr. Meek and my colleague Mrs. Pinter to calm me down and I hope -- I hope you didn't misunderstand me. I am a hot-blooded man. I react quickly. Perhaps that is how I was brought up. And I will therefore respond even though perhaps I should count to ten and say, "Well, easy, let's take it easy and we will clear it up." But it always seemed to me that I didn't have enough time, and I was so afraid that I never have time to explain it all because I realise how many things I would have to explain. And I do hope that we've explained it with the witnesses that we, the Defence, called, because otherwise, I do not know what it would have looked like in the end had they not come, had we not called here the highest -- the highest ranking political and military officials of the HZ HB, this horrible product, this terrible state, and at times I thought if somebody had seen me in this HZ HB, and just imagine at the Heliodrom had I had a client in the military investigative prison at the Heliodrom, the central military investigating prison, what if I had been seen there? And the OTP knows it. And there was yet another military investigating it prison in Ljubuski, and there was the central military investigating prison and the other one. I went there in 1993 because I had some clients - we could still do that at that time. We lawyers from Croatia could operate in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other way around. And had somebody seen me there and had they come down here to testify, would you believe that somebody said that "Well I've seen you at the Heliodrom too," and points at me. So what? Imagine now this feeling here in this courtroom with the picture that is being painted by the OTP and then saying, "Listen, wait, I was there because I was defending." I apologise to the interpreters, because I was telling myself all the time, you know, slowly, take it easy, this is your last chance, and yet I got carried away, so my apologies. And by the time I explained what I was doing there, do you know what kind of impression they would have got, especially in the early days when we still were too young, too green, before we fully understood what was going on and why couldn't I be at the Heliodrom and why couldn't my client, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, be at the Heliodrom? Why not? There were a couple of thousand soldiers at the Heliodrom and the central investigating Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prison was in two buildings, so of course, thousands of people came and went. So what? Are we really going to say before the world court -- can it really be used as an argument here, well, they happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time, and that's how it is, that's the way the cookie crumbles. And now you are to prove what you were doing there and what were you -- and what were you doing there? And then again, somebody says -- and now imagine somebody says that and says, "Ah-hah, you were not there because of this but because you were a commander of such and such unit," and then the ball starts rolling. And what about evidence? There were many such balls, many such pictures, many testimonies, many attitudes presented, never supported by any proof, by any argument, and I'm coming to that. What caused major problem for the Defence was that the indictment is vague and unclear, and we had to infer what was it that Mr. Mladen Naletilic was specifically charged with, at what time, on what day, did he commit which one of the acts and which of the acts with which he is being charged with, in which area did he act according to the indictment? Who are the individuals that he cooperated with in planning of the persecution, according to the OTP? Who are the individuals that he helped? Whom did he instigate and whom did he fail to punish? Your Honours, even as late as yesterday, that is at the very end of this case, but it does not come as a surprise to me any longer. But my client, Mladen Naletilic, and I learned that he was responsible for two more waves of persecution. They have never been mentioned before. Yesterday, for the first time, these two new waves of persecution were specified referring to the dates of 13th and 14th of June, 1993, and the 29th of September, 1993. Nothing new and everything is perfectly fits into the manner of operation of the OTP. But we ask whether one can really -- when the case is at the end and at the moment when the closing argument is presented, can one really at that point articulate clearly and loudly what Mr. Mladen Naletilic is held responsible for? Throughout, the OTP has been claiming something, and the Defence would dearly like to know on what evidence -- what is the evidence underpinning these claims? For instance, Your Honours, where is the proof that Mr. Mladen Naletilic was Mate Boban's friend? When was such evidence produced? Through which witness? Through which document? And even that is not enough. It is even said that he -- that he voiced an opinion, but they do not say "opinion". They mention racist statements. Please, I will remind you of the incident in question. It is Witness O who says that at some informal, or perhaps even a formal meeting, at Mate Boban's, a man was present and listen how important he is, it's only when he left he learned subsequently - and of course you will see, but you must have already analysed his testimony that he learned that it was -- it had been Mladen Naletilic. He must have been very important if he learned that only later on, except that I do not know who he talked to, who described and identified that man, and how did he learn that that was Mr. Naletilic. But that was his testimony and allegedly Mladen Naletilic said to him, and now please listen to this racist statement, that in his view, Muslims were Croats of Islamic faith. Well, right up to 1974, 92, and to this day, some people declared themselves in this way, and throughout the history that was the only way they could identify themselves, ethnically, and I do know. I fail to see what is racist about it. I ask you, a German, a believing German, he's a Muslim, and yet he's a German and he's been a German for generations. What is his ethnic background, a German; and what is his faith, why, Islam. But that is how pieces are put together and that is how the OTP puts pieces together, these are the testimonies and these are opinions, and the evidence is no where to be found. We, the Defence, would dearly like to know where from did the OTP get this information, because there is absolutely no evidence that -- so that there was yet another operation in Sovici and Doljani a couple of days after the death of Mario Hrkac, Cikota. We can recall a witness who testified about this operation. When was that? A couple of days after Mr. Hrkac's death. Which of the OTP witnesses or defence witnesses and which document was used to support this claim? Not a single one. Yes, there is one. And he is called Falk Simang, who when asked by Your Honours how did he get to Doljani answered by road. And when Your Honours asked, "Well, where did this road go?" He said, "Well, it got to Doljani." And I can remember how Your Honours showed him a map because one cannot get to Doljani except through Sovici, and he does not even know that such a place exists. Now, we can -- do we conclude that he dropped by parachute or that he never was there? Well, he didn't drop there by parachute, that we know, so he obviously was not there because he could not go anywhere without his interpreter because he didn't know a single word in Croatian, and he's the only one who said something about the 23rd or 24th, and in point of fact -- no, I do not even want to comment him because you heard his testimony. Today we know a great deal more than at the time when he testified. A man who is ready for money, for dollars, to kill once; the second time he does it to lay his hands on a car, and a Skoda at that, and is not ready to lie? No, no. You know, a murder is a severe crime but lying, no, no, he wouldn't. Especially if he's been sentenced twice for life and when OTP delegations went to Germany to talk him into coming here to testify. He was also the only witness testifying to the fact that my client was the commander of the Convicts Battalion in 1993. Him and Mr. Rudiger, who was also given a life sentence for the same murder and for the snatching of the same Skoda car. Your Honours, I would simply not go into that. I realise only now why they were brought here, simply there was nobody else. If the OTP had a choice, if they had had a choice, they would have never called these two. They were forced to do that. This is where we stand. The accused are here, the OTP knows that the accused shouldn't be here, but let's play our game to the end and see what good may come out of that. Can you please just imagine, for a brief moment, for somebody to say that in May, Cikota was in Mostar together with him, and not even to mention everything else that that witness said. Ralf Rudiger, his colleague, his brother in crime, his fellow murderer, replied to my question whether his trial could be renewed if the command responsibility of Mr. Naletilic could be proven, so his reply was yes. My opinion, to be honest, is that this wouldn't be so bad, because he still stands a chance of redeeming himself before God. I'm talking about the second man, but I don't have any hopes for the first person that I've mentioned. And now let's move on. We read the closing brief. We heard the closing argument, and out of the 56 OTP witnesses, finally the OTP singled out six of those who testified in order to prove Mr. Naletilic's guilt. And the last one, the sixth on that list, is the person who has been dead for three years, and testimonies by the dead are taken into account in every legal system, that is a well-known fact, isn't it? Obviously I'm talking about Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Republic of Croatia -- the late President of the Republic of Croatia. The OTP, however, forgets one thing, and that is that it has been said before this Trial Chamber on several occasions, and it has been read in several documents, that it was the international community that asked Franjo Tudjman to intervene in order to bring the conflict in Bosnia to an end. The conflict between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. Croats even gave him the power of attorney to represent them, and whenever he represented them, he represented them on behalf of the international community. And I believe that it is another well-known fact, why would OTP want to distort that picture? They are the only ones who can answer that question. The most dangerous thing in any interpretation, in any speech, and especially in accusing somebody, is to take things out of a context, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. take sentences out of a context, and then base, allegations about somebody's guilt on these sentences taken out of the context. In that, it doesn't really make any difference whether this is based on a transcript of a conversation or a meeting or on another written document. If it is indeed the OTP's position that proof for Mladen Naletilic's guilt and for the existence of an international nature of the conflict between Muslims and Croats are presidential transcripts; then by respecting the rules of fair trial and the rules that every evidence should be presented before the accused, the OTP should have called, as witnesses, the participants of those meetings who are still alive. The participants in these meetings would testify to the alleged conversations which according to the OTP prove that Croatia was indeed involved in the war between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that by that involvement, the conflict could be characterised as an international conflict. The OTP has had at its disposal all the possible mechanisms to bring these witnesses before this trial, and it also had the burden of proof to do so, but it was the Defence that did that, and you will remember how impatient we were in waiting for the OTP to do things like that. I remember Milan Kovac who mentioned that he was in Split at a meeting with Mr. Tudjman. That is what the OTP put to him. And then Mr. Kovac said, "No, I was never there." And then we waited for the OTP to come up with some evidence, newspaper article or something like that, but they didn't come up with anything, and now, about the presidential transcripts, how were they authorised? Only through living witnesses they could have been authorised. The Defence was the one that has done that, and the OTP, on the other hand, has not done it, has not respected that mechanism. And let's move on. The OTP refers to President Tudjman and draws a parallel with Slobodan Milosevic, and I really don't know how the OTP did that. We did not hear any witness, we did not hear any piece of evidence that would prove that there were agreements between Tudjman and Milosevic. If they had wanted, they could have called Milosevic. He is here. He's in his courtroom in this Tribunal every day and we heard him testifying in his courtroom, but here, the OTP could say whatever they wanted to say but if they wanted to allege something, they should have provided evidence to prove that. Then they also said that both Tudjman and Milosevic played an active role in Bosnia-Herzegovina but they failed to mention Alija Izetbegovic in all that. Was there no Alija Izetbegovic? Did he not play a role? Was he not important? Or the OTP deliberately failed to mention his name in all that? If the OTP was objective, then they could have made all of our lives easier, especially bearing in mind the fact that they will not be able to change history. They should have said yes, there were three sides to this conflict, each of them with their own respective interests. There was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the Muslim army, the HVO as the Croatian Army, and the Army of Republika Srpska as the Serbian army. Until the very last moment, the BH Army was deliberately ignored and it was alleged all the time that all the attacks were attacks on civilians, Muslims civilians, and at the same time, the BH Army had over 300.000 men and at the same time, the HVO had the strength of about 30.000 men. Alija Izetbegovic, who was deliberately ignored by the OTP for the reasons known only to them, so that person, Alija Izetbegovic, in 1993 or 1994 - I apologise, if the year is wrong - but it is a well-known fact. So in that year, he was tried, together with some other people, in Sarajevo for fundamentalist ideas and an attempt to create a Muslim state. In 1990, he ascended to power with the same people who he had been tried with, when he came out of the prison, but now his policy changed. He opted for a democratic Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was the only one who wanted to do that, according to the OTP, who he -- he was the only one who was worthy of that mission, and all the other peoples, i.e., representatives of the other peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were evil, and that same person had spent ten years in prison in the then Yugoslavia because of his ideas, which had nothing to do with multi-culturalism and multi-ethnic ideas. He wrote -- he is the author of the Islam Declaration, and I'm just going to quote one sentence from that declaration, for which he was tried in Sarajevo. "We need to wait and us Muslims, we have to wait to -- in order to become a majority population in Bosnia, and when that happens, we will create an Islamic state." These are his words in the Islamic Declaration. So that same person set up the SDA. He won in the elections, and everything was -- before that was forgotten, as if he had nothing whatsoever to do with anything that had happened previously, as if the BH Army had nothing to do with what had happened before. But we will move on to that later on. And now, we have five witnesses that the OTP singled out and the five that have remained after we have eliminated the last one, the sixth one, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and the OTP stresses their testimonies. But these five witnesses do not have any direct knowledge about Mladen Naletilic, about his role in the Convicts Battalion, whether he was the commander of the Convicts Battalion, about his possible negative attitude towards the Muslims, whether he was carrying out ethnic cleansing. One of these witnesses, Grinten, on the contrary, pointed out that it was Mladen Naletilic who tried to provide protection for two Muslim villages in the heart of Herzegovina on the road from Mostar to Siroki Brijeg. Would this have been done by the person who wanted to cleanse the Herzegovinian area from Muslims? The other four witnesses, I will talk about their testimonies in detail later on, everything that the Defence said they would do, we did. We brought before this Court the most prominent military and civilian persons of the HZ HB, and they offered to this Trial Chamber the picture of the events that had preceded these events, during the conflict, and after the conflict. The Defence has called the witnesses who had answers to all the key questions. The witnesses who participated directly in decision-making, who had very important roles and who participated in the decision-making process. So they were the one who is made decision. They were the ones who implemented these decisions, and they testified in this courtroom publicly. None of these witnesses confirmed the allegations in the indictment about the role of Mladen Naletilic, and his position. They did not confirm this as the witnesses to the events which are the subject of the indictment, as -- and as the direct participants in the events which are the subject of the indictment. Therefore, we should say this: Following these testimonies, if one undertakes a careful analysis, one will see that the OTP is not right when they say that Mladen Naletilic was the commander of the Convicts Battalion in 1993, i.e., at the time indicated in the indictment. I'm going to be referring only to that time which is indicated in the indictment, because I believe that nobody -- neither us nor the Trial Chamber -- is interested in anything else but the things which are specified in the indictment. Further on, that the Convicts Battalion committed crimes in Sovici and Doljani in April in 1993, under the command of Mladen Naletilic. Do we have any proof that the Convicts Battalion committed any crimes at all, that Mladen Naletilic had his subordinates over which he had the real military and civilian power; that Mladen Naletilic had any military or political role, that he participated in the persecution of Muslims from Mostar in May and July, 1993; that he used prisoners of war as human shields and in forced labour; that he tortured, abused, or in any other way illegally treated the prisoners of war of the Muslim army; that he personally ordered the destruction of Muslim property and setting their property on fire; that during the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, that is, of the two armies of the same state, their conflict had the nature of an international conflict. In a nutshell, the Defence believes that the OTP, on which the burden of the proof lies, that the OTP failed to prove beyond reasonable Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. doubt that Mladen Naletilic had the role assigned to him by the Prosecution and that he is responsible for the crimes that he is charged with. What is the quality of the OTP evidence and the thesis put forth in the indictment? The Defence is aware that the OTP has different views on the events than the Defence does. But the Defence also has to say that the OTP has not invested any effort in order to establish the facts. If the Prosecutor had tried to do so, this Trial Chamber would have been given a completely different picture of the events. It would have had totally different persons as accused. Your Honours, I believe that we have established, after hearing three investigators from the OTP team, these three said to my question that they never cooperated with anybody else but the government of -- or the authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When I asked them who these authorities were, when I asked them to name them, these three investigators said it was the AID, the secret Muslim political police. All three of them said that. Now, I wonder how was it that the OTP carried out its investigation? Let's imagine you have to go to Mostar, you don't speak the language, you approach somebody and say, "I am from the ICTY. What happened?" So how do you imagine that these investigations were carried out? Let me tell you. It was really very simple. The AID organised and prepared everything and offered as if on a platter, everything they found suitable. At the same time, the Prosecution did not verify any of these facts or evidence with the other side, because they didn't want to do that. They should have wanted to do that if they had done that, then these proceedings would not have lasted 14 months, my client, Mladen Naletilic, would never be here. But let's say that even if Mladen Naletilic was here and if the OTP behaved differently, then these proceedings would last -- have lasted a maximum of two months. It was the AID that brought the witnesses and offered evidence that the OTP just accepted. Why? Because the AID wanted to mask their own crimes and they did that by forging an alliance with the most powerful organisation in the world, which chooses who to accuse, who not to accuse. Let me draw a parallel which is very fresh in my mind. I am clearly telling you here that Sovici and Doljani, which are the subjects of this indictment, are just a story for little children. No civilian was murdered, nobody was raped there, nobody was killed there. And something that the BH Army did three months later, and the three months later the BH Army massacred 35 civilians, they slaughtered their throats, they slashed their throats, 35 civilians were massacred three months later, they took women and children to the Jablanica camp. We heard testimonies to that effect. Six-month-old babies, five-year-old children were exchanged a few months later, and all the men stayed in the camp until the exchange which took place in the -- in 1994. And there is no indictment for that evil, for that crime, and I assure you there never will be, and can you imagine how the people reacted when they were listening to this procedure, how they must felt when the OTP wanted to proclaim that atrocious place, the camp in Jablanica, a refugee camp, and the operation which was the event during a terrible massacre happened. They didn't want to mention, and there will never be an indictment for that. And if that was not the case, would then, Mr. Safet Idrizovic have given testimony here as a rebuttal witness, if the OTP had been objective and if it had accused the BH -- criminals from the BH Army, the alliance would have been interrupted and there would have been no more witnesses in this case. Let me not even mention all the things which happened in Konjic, Prozor, Jablanica, long ago, long before the 16th of April, long before the 9th of May. I believe that we have come to the break. The Croats had already been cleansed, already incarcerated, both soldiers and the civilians were in the various camps long before the 16th of April. Your Honours, I believe -- I believe it is the time for our next break, and I will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will break here and we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. During the break, I went through my papers and I seem to have been carried away again. There are very many things that I still have to say and I'm not sure I'll be able to make it by the time of adjournment, but that's how I am. Of course, two and a half hours, you must realise yourselves how difficult it is to summarise all that happened during these 14 months. But I place my trust in you and I hope that my closing argument and all that I will say will certainly not be the basis on which you will pass your judgement. You will pass your judgement on the basis of the evidence and the sense that you will read into it. We adjourned at a time when I was speaking about the crime in Doljani committed by the BH Army three months after the events in Sovici and Doljani referred to in the indictment.
